Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On October 18, 2023, the Federal Reserve released its findings from the 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances, which documented significant and persistent racial disparities in wealth and income. [2, 3, 9] The report revealed that the median wealth of a typical White family ($285,000) was approximately six times that of a typical Black family ($44,900) and five times that of a typical Hispanic family ($61,600). [2, 7] The analysis presented a nuanced view of the wealth gap's evolution since 2019: while wealth for the typical Black and Hispanic family grew at a faster percentage rate (61% and 47%, respectively) than for the typical White family (31%), causing the wealth ratios to narrow slightly, the absolute dollar gap widened. [2, 7] For instance, the dollar gap in median wealth between White and Black families increased by about $50,000. [2, 4] In contrast to wealth, income disparities widened, as the inflation-adjusted median income for White families rose 1% between 2019 and 2022, while it fell by 2% for Black families and 1% for Hispanic families. [2] <2> In what was described as the largest healthcare worker strike in U.S. history, over 75,000 Kaiser Permanente employees began a three-day strike on October 4, 2023. [1, 4, 9] The strike, organized by the Coalition of Kaiser Permanente Unions, involved a wide range of staff, including nurses, technicians, and support personnel, across facilities in California, Colorado, Oregon, Washington, Virginia, and Washington, D.C. [1, 2, 3] The central issues driving the work stoppage were demands for increased pay and solutions to a severe staffing crisis that the unions argued was compromising patient care. [2, 3, 4] The planned three-day strike concluded, and after negotiations resumed, a tentative agreement was announced on October 13, 2023. [2, 5, 10] The four-year agreement, included a 21% wage increase over the contract's term and established minimum hourly wages of $25 in California and $23 in other states. [5, 6, 12, 17] It also contained provisions to improve staffing levels and limit outsourcing. [5, 12, 17] <3> On September 28, 2023, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 1228 into law, mandating a new minimum wage for employees of fast-food chains with at least 60 locations nationwide. [3, 4, 6] This legislation, increased the minimum wage for over 500,000 fast-food workers in the state to $20 per hour. [2, 7, 8] The law also established a Fast Food Council to advise on future annual wage increases and working conditions until 2029. [2, 4, 9] The bill was the result of a compromise that replaced a more expansive proposal, AB 257, and aimed to address long-standing calls for higher wages and better conditions in the industry. [3, 4] <4> Federal Reserve data confirmed that the wealthiest 20% of Americans were in a better financial position than before the COVID-19 pandemic, while the bottom 80% saw their excess savings depleted. A primary reason for the wealth increase among the affluent was the ability to accumulate substantial savings during lockdown periods, bolstered by government financial support. As of June 2023, cash savings for the top quintile were still approximately 8% above their pre-COVID levels. In contrast, bank deposits and other assets for the bottom 80% of households fell below their March 2020 levels. Analysis of net worth changes during the pandemic showed that richer households saw a median increase of $172,200, whereas half of the poorer households had a net worth of $500 or less by the end of 2021, a modest gain from a pre-pandemic net worth of zero or less. <5> On September 12, 2023, the U.S. Census Bureau released its annual reports on income, poverty, and health insurance, including the report 'Income in the United States: 2022', which covers data for the 2022 calendar year. [2, 3] The report revealed that real median household income fell 2.3% from 2021 to $74,580 in 2022. [2] Notably, based on pretax money income, the Gini index, a standard measure of income inequality, decreased by 1.2% from 0.494 in 2021 to 0.488 in 2022. [1, 2] This marked the first statistically significant annual decrease in the Gini index since 2007. [1, 2] The reduction in inequality was attributed to declines in real income at the middle and top of the income distribution. [1] In contrast, post-tax income calculations showed an increase in inequality. [1] The report also noted that the official poverty rate of 11.5% was not statistically different from 2021 and that the number of people without health insurance decreased. <6> In a report from the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities (CBPP) published on August 29, 2023, it was highlighted that government pandemic-era policies had a significant impact on reducing poverty in 2020 and 2021. These economic security programs prevented 53 million people from falling into poverty over those two years, turning what could have been a record surge in poverty into historic declines. [1, 4] The report warned that with the expiration of this temporary aid, poverty had likely increased in 2022, and that official data from the Census Bureau was expected in September 2023. [2, 3] A subsequent analysis confirmed this prediction, revealing that the Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM) poverty rate rose from 8.0 percent to 12.4 percent in 2022, largely driven by the end of the expanded Child Tax Credit and stimulus payments. [5] <7> On August 10, 2023, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) published a report titled 'Visualizing the Racial Wealth Gap'. [1, 3] The report details how systemic inequities and institutional barriers prevent people of color from attaining economic security through employment, education, and homeownership. [1, 3] These factors, according to the ACLU, have resulted in significant and persistent wealth disparities between different racial groups, creating a massive racial wealth gap in the United States. [3] The report highlights homeownership as a primary method for building intergenerational wealth and notes that the gap in homeownership between Black and white families grew from 25% in 1976 to 30% in 2022. [1, 3] <8> JPMorgan Chase has announced philanthropic commitments totaling $6.7 million aimed at closing the racial wealth gap and promoting inclusive growth. [2] This initiative is part of the firm's broader $30 billion Racial Equity Commitment. [2] The funding includes $1.7 million for non-profit organizations in the greater Boston area to foster economic opportunity and wealth creation by providing technical assistance and educational programs to small business owners and entrepreneurs of color. [2, 3] A separate $5 million national commitment will go to the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) to establish four new think tanks called C-HOPE (Centers of Innovation). [2, 3] These centers will focus on advancing innovative solutions for health equity, inclusive economic growth, education, and climate justice. [2] The announcement coincided with the second anniversary of the opening of Chase's Community Center Branch in Mattapan, Massachusetts. [2] <9> A report from JUST Capital, published on July 21, 2023, suggests a tentative reduction in income inequality in the United States. [2] The analysis, which references data up to June 2023, found that the income for the lowest-earning 50% of Americans grew by 4.5% over the preceding 12 months, a significantly higher rate than the 1.2% average for all Americans. [2] Furthermore, the report highlighted that in the year leading up to June 2023, real average hourly wages, which account for inflation, increased by 1.2%. [2, 3]

[1] The report identified housing equity as the primary driver for wealth gains among Black households. [2, 4] In contrast to wealth, income disparities widened, as the inflation-adjusted median income for White families rose 1% between 2019 and 2022, while it fell by 2% for Black families and 1% for Hispanic families. [2]

metadata.original_text: This time series records income inequality data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2024-03-17 to 2024-06-02. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> Based on the Federal Reserve's 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances, released in October 2023, the financial landscape of American households has shown significant shifts. From 2019 to 2022, the median household net worth surged by 37%, reaching $192,900. Despite this overall growth, substantial racial wealth disparities persist. In 2022, the median net worth for White households was $285,000, over six times that of Black households, which stood at $44,900. While Black households saw a notable 60% increase in their median wealth during this period, the absolute dollar gap between White and Black households widened. The primary driver for the overall wealth increase was the appreciation in housing values. Concurrently, data on business ownership presents a mixed picture. A Brookings Institution analysis of Census Bureau data indicates that the number of Black-owned employer firms grew by 4.72% between 2019 and 2020. Other reports show varied growth rates in subsequent years, with one study noting a 20.8% increase in Black-owned employer businesses from 2021 to 2022 alone. <2> A Brookings Institution analysis of the Federal Reserve's 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances, published in January 2024, revealed that while the median wealth for Black households grew from $27,970 in 2019 to $44,890 in 2022, the absolute wealth gap compared to white households also increased. [1] The total difference in wealth between the median white household and the median Black household expanded by $49,950, reaching a total of $240,120. [1] The report identified housing equity as the primary driver for wealth gains among Black households. In contrast, increases in wealth for white households were more significantly influenced by corporate and business equity, a factor that exacerbated the overall racial wealth gap. [1] <3> The Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) released the 7th edition of its 'Who Pays?' report, a state-by-state distributional analysis of tax systems. The report, which examines tax laws as of January 1, 2024, found that tax systems in 44 states worsen income inequality by requiring the lowest-income individuals to pay a higher percentage of their income in state and local taxes than the wealthiest residents. On average, the lowest-income 20 percent of taxpayers face a state and local tax rate that is almost 60 percent higher than the rate for the top 1 percent of households. The analysis further specified that 41 states tax their wealthiest 1 percent less than their bottom 20 percent, and 46 states tax the top 1 percent less than the middle 20 percent. <4> On January 1, 2024, minimum wage increases went into effect in 22 states, raising wages for an estimated 9.9 million workers. The raises are part of a larger trend of states and municipalities independently increasing their wage floors, as the federal minimum wage has remained at $7.25 per hour since 2009. Many of these state-level increases are the result of automatic adjustments for inflation or previously scheduled legislative action. For example, new laws in Maryland accelerated a planned increase to $15 an hour, which took effect on January 1, 2024. In total, 25 states were scheduled to increase their minimum wage throughout 2024, with Florida, Nevada, and Oregon implementing their raises later in the year. With these changes, seven states and Washington D.C. now have a minimum wage of at least $15 per hour. <5> The Prenatal-to-3 Policy Impact Center issued a brief detailing state-level minimum wage policies and their effect on families. The report, which reflects data as of October 1, 2023, found that 29 states, or just over half, have implemented a minimum wage of at least $10.00 per hour. The brief underscores the significance of higher state minimum wages in boosting household income, mitigating child poverty, and enhancing children's health and development. It also noted that throughout 2023, 30 states introduced legislation to either further raise their minimum wage or do away with subminimum wages for specific worker populations. <6> On November 30, 2023, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) released its report on Personal Income and Outlays for the month of October 2023. The data revealed a 0.2% increase in personal income, equivalent to $57.1 billion, and a 0.3% rise in disposable personal income (DPI), amounting to $63.4 billion. The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, a key inflation gauge, saw a minimal increase of less than 0.1% for the month. On an annual basis, the PCE price index rose by 3.0% compared to October 2022. These figures offer a crucial macroeconomic snapshot of American income and spending patterns. <7> The Circle of Protection, a broad coalition of Christian organizations and ministries in the U.S., initiated a campaign to make poverty and hunger key issues in the 2024 presidential election. The initiative formally asks all Democratic and Republican candidates to submit video statements outlining their plans to create opportunities for and provide assistance to people experiencing poverty and hunger. This is the fourth presidential election cycle, starting in 2012, that the group has undertaken such an effort. While most candidates have responded in previous years, the 2024 campaign has seen slower participation, particularly from leading candidates. <8> On November 15, 2023, the Institute for Policy Studies (IPS) released a report titled 'The True Cost of Billionaire Philanthropy'. The report, authored by Helen Flannery, Chuck Collins, and Bella DeVaan, is part of the institute's 'Gilded Giving' series and argues that ultra-wealthy individuals use philanthropy to avoid taxes and increase their societal influence, with taxpayers subsidizing these donations. Specifically, the analysis details how wealthy donors utilize intermediaries like private foundations and donor-advised funds (DAFs) to gain immediate tax deductions while often delaying the distribution of funds to active charities. A key finding of the report is that the collective wealth of 73 U.S. billionaires who signed the Giving Pledge in 2010 grew by 138 percent (or 224 percent adjusted for inflation) by 2022, increasing from $348 billion to $828 billion. The authors assert that taxpayers effectively contribute significantly to these donations; for every dollar a billionaire donates, taxpayers lose 74 cents in revenue due to deductions for income, capital gains, and estate taxes. <9> In her book 'Fair Enough?: Support for Redistribution in the Age of Inequality,' author Charlotte Cavaillé examines a puzzling trend in several post-industrial democracies: despite rising income and wealth inequality, there has not been a corresponding surge in public demand for more egalitarian policies. [1] Cavaillé specifically notes that in the United States, the gap in attitudes toward redistribution between low-income and high-income voters is narrowing, and in Great Britain, public support for such policies is actually decreasing. [1] The book challenges the conventional assumption that growing economic disparity will automatically trigger political pressure for greater redistribution. [1] Instead, Cavaillé proposes a new framework arguing that attitudes are shaped by both material self-interest and shared norms of fairness. [1, 8] The book concludes that while policy changes are possible, they are unlikely to be driven by a public opinion shift in favor of redistribution. <10> On October 18, 2023, the Federal Reserve released its findings from the 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances, which documented significant and persistent racial disparities in wealth and income. [2, 3, 9] The report revealed that the median wealth of a typical White family ($285,000) was approximately six times that of a typical Black family ($44,900) and five times that of a typical Hispanic family ($61,600). [2, 7] The analysis presented a nuanced view of the wealth gap's evolution since 2019: while wealth for the typical Black and Hispanic family grew at a faster percentage rate (61% and 47%, respectively) than for the typical White family (31%), causing the wealth ratios to narrow slightly, the absolute dollar gap widened. [2, 7] For instance, the dollar gap in median wealth between White and Black families increased by about $50,000. [2, 4] In contrast to wealth, income disparities widened, as the inflation-adjusted median income for White families rose 1% between 2019 and 2022, while it fell by 2% for Black families and 1% for Hispanic families. [2]

The report, which reflects data as of October 1, 2023, found that 29 states, or just over half, have implemented a minimum wage of at least $10.00 per hour. The brief underscores the significance of higher state minimum wages in boosting household income, mitigating child poverty, and enhancing children's health and development. It also noted that throughout 2023, 30 states introduced legislation to either further raise their minimum wage or do away with subminimum wages for specific worker populations. <9> On November 30, 2023, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) released its report on Personal Income and Outlays for the month of October 2023. The data revealed a 0.2% increase in personal income, equivalent to $57.1 billion, and a 0.3% rise in disposable personal income (DPI), amounting to $63.4 billion. The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, a key inflation gauge, saw a minimal increase of less than 0.1% for the month. On an annual basis, the PCE price index rose by 3.0% compared to October 2022. These figures offer a crucial macroeconomic snapshot of American income and spending patterns.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> A report from Digital Weekday, published on June 22, 2024, highlighted significant and persistent wealth and income inequality in the United States, with a notable racial wealth gap. The analysis, which utilized 2022 data from the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances, indicated that the median wealth for white families was $285,000. [1, 5, 6] In comparison, the median wealth for Black families was approximately $45,000, and for Hispanic families, it was about $61,000-$62,000. [1, 5, 10] Federal Reserve data confirms these large disparities, showing the typical white family had about six times the wealth of the typical Black family and five times that of the typical Hispanic family in 2022. [6] Although the absolute dollar-value gap in wealth between white families and Black and Hispanic families grew between 2019 and 2022, the wealth of the typical Black and Hispanic family saw a greater percentage increase during that period. [6] <2> The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) released its 'Society at a Glance 2024' report on June 20, 2024, which provides an overview of social indicators across member countries. [1] The report finds that among OECD countries, the United States has one of the highest levels of income and wealth inequality. [3] It specifically highlights that household wealth is significantly more concentrated than income, with the top 10% of households in the United States owning 79% of the country's total household wealth. [3] In comparison, the average for OECD countries is 52%. [3] Income inequality in the U.S. was also noted as among the highest in the OECD, alongside Chile, Costa Rica, and Türkiye. [3] <3> In the first quarter of 2024, the wealthiest 1% of earners in the United States held 30.6% of the country's total net worth, according to the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED). This figure is part of the Distributional Financial Accounts, which are published quarterly and integrate data from the Financial Accounts of the United States and the Survey of Consumer Finances to provide a comprehensive view of wealth distribution. The data for the first quarter of 2024, which concluded on March 31, 2024, was officially released on June 14, 2024, highlighting the ongoing concentration of wealth at the top of the economic spectrum. <4> On June 12, 2024, Sarah Anderson testified before the U.S. Senate Budget Committee during a hearing titled, "Making Wall Street Pay Its Fair Share: Raising Revenue, Strengthening Our Economy." Anderson, in her capacity as the Global Economy Program Director at the Institute for Policy Studies and co-editor of Inequality.org, spoke on the necessity of tax reforms to address wealth disparity. She advocated for several proposals, including implementing higher taxes on companies with significant pay gaps between CEOs and median workers, enacting a financial transaction tax, and increasing the tax rate on stock buybacks. The hearing, chaired by Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, also featured testimony from other experts like Nobel Prize-winning economist Joseph Stiglitz and explored the deep partisan divisions on taxing corporations and high-income individuals ahead of the 2025 debates on expiring tax provisions. <5> A study by researchers affiliated with the Samuel DuBois Cook Center for Social Equity at Duke University found that the mean net worth gap between Black and white households in the U.S. grew by 38% from 2019 to 2022. The paper, titled "Setting the Record Straight on Racial Wealth Inequality," was published in the May 2024 issue of AEA Papers and Proceedings. This increase brought the mean wealth gap to approximately $1.15 million. The research, which analyzed data from the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances, challenges the view that factors like educational attainment are the primary drivers of the wealth gap. Instead, the authors point to the cumulative impact of U.S. racial history and the intergenerational transfer of wealth as more significant factors. <6> The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) released its revised data for the first quarter of 2024, showing a continued decline in the labor share of national income for non-farm workers to 55.8%. This figure is part of a longer-term downward trend from 64.1% in the first quarter of 2001, indicating that wages are not keeping pace with productivity growth. [2] The revised report for Q1 2024, published on June 6, 2024, indicated that nonfarm business sector labor productivity increased by 0.2 percent, a downward revision from the preliminary estimate of 0.3 percent. [1, 2] Unit labor costs saw a 4.0 percent increase, which was also a downward revision from the initial 4.7 percent estimate. [1, 2] <7> In a historic victory for the United Auto Workers (UAW), workers at the Volkswagen plant in Chattanooga, Tennessee, voted overwhelmingly to unionize. [1, 3, 4] The election, overseen by the National Labor Relations Board, took place from April 17 to April 19, 2024. [2, 5] The final tally, announced on April 19, 2024, was 2,628 in favor of joining the UAW and 985 against, with 73% of voters supporting unionization. [2, 6, 7] This outcome marks a significant breakthrough for the UAW's campaign to organize foreign-owned auto plants in the southern United States, a region that has historically been resistant to unionization, making it the first such plant in the South to unionize via an election since the 1940s. [3, 6] <8> A multi-national study titled "Measuring Absolute Income Mobility: Lessons from North America and Europe" was published in the April 2024 issue of the American Economic Journal: Applied Economics. The research, involving academics from several institutions including a faculty associate from the University of Michigan's Stone Center for Inequality Dynamics, analyzed absolute income mobility for birth cohorts from 1960-1987 in eight countries. The findings indicate a varied landscape of economic opportunity; while the United States and Canada have seen upward mobility rates decline to around 50% for recent cohorts, countries like Norway and Finland maintained rates above 70%. The study confirms a decades-long decline in the U.S., where fewer individuals earn more than their parents, a trend largely driven by lower income growth and rising inequality. While the final paper was published in 2024, earlier working paper versions of the research were available as early as 2020. <9> On National Equal Pay Day, March 12, 2024, the U.S. Census Bureau highlighted updated data on the gender pay gap. [1, 3] The data, from the year 2022, showed that women working full-time, year-round earned a median of 84.0 cents for every dollar earned by men. [1, 2, 4] This figure represents the narrowest the gender pay gap has been on record, though it marks a slow progression over nearly five decades. [2, 4] For comparison, in 1973, women earned 56.6 cents to a man's dollar, indicating a gain of 27.4 cents over 49 years. [1] President Joe Biden officially proclaimed March 12, 2024, as National Equal Pay Day, underscoring the ongoing fight for pay equity despite the progress. [3]

Prediction target period: from 2024-09-01 to 2024-11-17. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> A technical note by economists Thomas Piketty, Emmanuel Saez, and Gabriel Zucman was published, offering a commentary on the 2024 income inequality estimates from Gerald Auten and David Splinter. The authors report identifying an empirical error in how untaxed partnership income is allocated in Auten and Splinter's analysis. They argue that this income, which has increased due to more generous fiscal depreciation rules, was incorrectly assigned to owners of sole proprietorships rather than to the wealthier owners of partnerships. Piketty, Saez, and Zucman posit that this misallocation results in a bias in the level and growth of the top 1% income share. This critique is part of an ongoing academic debate, with the authors having commented on earlier drafts of Auten and Splinter's work and Auten and Splinter having previously responded. <2> In a policy brief published on July 30, 2024, the Grand Challenges for Social Work initiative outlined several recommendations to combat extreme economic inequality in the United States. The initiative, which notes that the U.S. ranks at the top for both income and wealth inequality among high-income nations, put forth these proposals ahead of a major election year to help focus policy advocacy. The recommendations detailed in the brief include creating an income floor for all citizens, modernizing the federal minimum wage, and ending consumption taxes on basic necessities. Further proposals consist of facilitating free and efficient income tax filing, stabilizing Social Security financing, eliminating student debt, supporting entrepreneurship, and funding reparations for slavery and other anti-Black policies. <3> A report from Digital Weekday, published on June 22, 2024, highlighted significant and persistent wealth and income inequality in the United States, with a notable racial wealth gap. The analysis, which utilized 2022 data from the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances, indicated that the median wealth for white families was $285,000. [1, 5, 6] In comparison, the median wealth for Black families was approximately $45,000, and for Hispanic families, it was about $61,000-$62,000. [1, 5, 10] Federal Reserve data confirms these large disparities, showing the typical white family had about six times the wealth of the typical Black family and five times that of the typical Hispanic family in 2022. [6] Although the absolute dollar-value gap in wealth between white families and Black and Hispanic families grew between 2019 and 2022, the wealth of the typical Black and Hispanic family saw a greater percentage increase during that period. [6] <4> The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) released its 'Society at a Glance 2024' report on June 20, 2024, which provides an overview of social indicators across member countries. [1] The report finds that among OECD countries, the United States has one of the highest levels of income and wealth inequality. [3] It specifically highlights that household wealth is significantly more concentrated than income, with the top 10% of households in the United States owning 79% of the country's total household wealth. [3] In comparison, the average for OECD countries is 52%. [3] Income inequality in the U.S. was also noted as among the highest in the OECD, alongside Chile, Costa Rica, and Türkiye. [3] <5> In the first quarter of 2024, the wealthiest 1% of earners in the United States held 30.6% of the country's total net worth, according to the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED). This figure is part of the Distributional Financial Accounts, which are published quarterly and integrate data from the Financial Accounts of the United States and the Survey of Consumer Finances to provide a comprehensive view of wealth distribution. The data for the first quarter of 2024, which concluded on March 31, 2024, was officially released on June 14, 2024, highlighting the ongoing concentration of wealth at the top of the economic spectrum. <6> On June 12, 2024, Sarah Anderson testified before the U.S. Senate Budget Committee during a hearing titled, "Making Wall Street Pay Its Fair Share: Raising Revenue, Strengthening Our Economy." Anderson, in her capacity as the Global Economy Program Director at the Institute for Policy Studies and co-editor of Inequality.org, spoke on the necessity of tax reforms to address wealth disparity. She advocated for several proposals, including implementing higher taxes on companies with significant pay gaps between CEOs and median workers, enacting a financial transaction tax, and increasing the tax rate on stock buybacks. The paper, titled "Setting the Record Straight on Racial Wealth Inequality," was published in the May 2024 issue of AEA Papers and Proceedings. This increase brought the mean wealth gap to approximately $1.15 million. The research, which analyzed data from the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances, challenges the view that factors like educational attainment are the primary drivers of the wealth gap. Instead, the authors point to the cumulative impact of U.S. racial history and the intergenerational transfer of wealth as more significant factors. <8> The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) released its revised data for the first quarter of 2024, showing a continued decline in the labor share of national income for non-farm workers to 55.8%. This figure is part of a longer-term downward trend from 64.1% in the first quarter of 2001, indicating that wages are not keeping pace with productivity growth. [2] The revised report for Q1 2024, published on June 6, 2024, indicated that nonfarm business sector labor productivity increased by 0.2 percent, a downward revision from the preliminary estimate of 0.3 percent. [1, 2] Unit labor costs saw a 4.0 percent increase, which was also a downward revision from the initial 4.7 percent estimate. [1, 2] <9> In a historic victory for the United Auto Workers (UAW), workers at the Volkswagen plant in Chattanooga, Tennessee, voted overwhelmingly to unionize. [1, 3, 4] The election, overseen by the National Labor Relations Board, took place from April 17 to April 19, 2024. [2, 5] The final tally, announced on April 19, 2024, was 2,628 in favor of joining the UAW and 985 against, with 73% of voters supporting unionization. [2, 6, 7] This outcome marks a significant breakthrough for the UAW's campaign to organize foreign-owned auto plants in the southern United States, a region that has historically been resistant to unionization, making it the first such plant in the South to unionize via an election since the 1940s. [3, 6]

metadata.original_text: This time series records income inequality data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2024-10-27 to 2025-01-12. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The World Bank has updated its Poverty and Inequality Platform (PIP) as of September 2024, with the data forming the basis for the forthcoming 'Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2024'. A significant enhancement in this update is the inclusion of 'nowcast' estimates for poverty at the country, regional, and global levels through 2024 for the first time. The updated database now contains nearly 2,400 surveys with the addition of 16 new country-years. This release also introduces new methodologies for gauging global poverty and new indicators for shared prosperity, such as the 'Prosperity Gap'. The 'Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2024', which was released on October 15, 2024, provides the first comprehensive assessment of global progress on poverty and shared prosperity since the COVID-19 pandemic. The report indicates that while global poverty reduction has resumed, the pace is slower than before the pandemic. It highlights that nearly 700 million people are living in extreme poverty (less than $2.15 a day), and progress has stalled due to slower economic growth and other crises. <2> On October 10, 2024, the Social Security Administration officially announced a 2.5 percent cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2025. This increase will impact more than 72.5 million individuals receiving Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits. Starting in January 2025, the average Social Security retirement benefit is set to increase by approximately $50 per month. <3> An analysis of Bureau of Economic Analysis and Census data by the Progressive Policy Institute (PPI) suggests a potential decrease in income inequality in the United States. The PPI report highlights that the national Gini coefficient, a standard measure of income distribution, peaked at 0.494 in 2021 before falling to 0.489 in 2022 and 0.485 in 2023, the lowest figure recorded since 2017. [8] This aligns with U.S. Census Bureau data which also reported a decrease in the Gini index to 0.488 in 2022 from 0.494 in 2021, marking the first decline since 2007. [8] Furthermore, the PPI analysis shows that the income share of the bottom three quintiles of the population rose from 24.8% in 2021 to 25.5% in 2023. <4> The U.S. Census Bureau released its 2023 data on income, poverty, and health insurance on September 10, 2024. The data showed that real median household income rose to $80,610 in 2023, a 4.0% increase from 2022 and the first significant annual rise since 2019. The official poverty rate decreased to 11.1% in 2023, down 0.4 percentage points from the previous year. However, the Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM), which considers government aid and necessary expenses, increased for the second consecutive year, rising to 12.9% from 12.4% in 2022. The percentage of the U.S. population without health insurance for all or part of 2023 was 8.0%, which was not a statistically significant change from the 7.9% rate in 2022. The press kit for the release included a variety of reports and analyses on these findings. <5> The Institute for Policy Studies (IPS) released its 30th annual "Executive Excess" report on August 29, 2024. [2, 7] The report, published on its Inequality.org project site, focuses on the 100 S&P 500 corporations with the lowest median worker pay, a group the report labels the 'Low-Wage 100'. [6, 7] A key finding highlights that from 2019 through 2023, these companies collectively spent $522 billion on stock buybacks. [7] The 2024 report also found that the average CEO-to-worker pay ratio at these firms was 538-to-1 in 2023, a decrease from 603-to-1 in 2022. [2] The average median worker pay at these companies was $34,522 in 2023, a 9% increase from the previous year. [1, 2, 7] The report suggests policy reforms such as taxing stock buybacks and levying higher taxes on corporations with extreme pay disparities. [2, 7] <6> A technical note by economists Thomas Piketty, Emmanuel Saez, and Gabriel Zucman was published, offering a commentary on the 2024 income inequality estimates from Gerald Auten and David Splinter. The authors report identifying an empirical error in how untaxed partnership income is allocated in Auten and Splinter's analysis. They argue that this income, which has increased due to more generous fiscal depreciation rules, was incorrectly assigned to owners of sole proprietorships rather than to the wealthier owners of partnerships. Piketty, Saez, and Zucman posit that this misallocation results in a bias in the level and growth of the top 1% income share. This critique is part of an ongoing academic debate, with the authors having commented on earlier drafts of Auten and Splinter's work and Auten and Splinter having previously responded. <7> In a policy brief published on July 30, 2024, the Grand Challenges for Social Work initiative outlined several recommendations to combat extreme economic inequality in the United States. The initiative, which notes that the U.S. ranks at the top for both income and wealth inequality among high-income nations, put forth these proposals ahead of a major election year to help focus policy advocacy. The recommendations detailed in the brief include creating an income floor for all citizens, modernizing the federal minimum wage, and ending consumption taxes on basic necessities. Further proposals consist of facilitating free and efficient income tax filing, stabilizing Social Security financing, eliminating student debt, supporting entrepreneurship, and funding reparations for slavery and other anti-Black policies. <8> A report from Digital Weekday, published on June 22, 2024, highlighted significant and persistent wealth and income inequality in the United States, with a notable racial wealth gap. The analysis, which utilized 2022 data from the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances, indicated that the median wealth for white families was $285,000. [1, 5, 6] In comparison, the median wealth for Black families was approximately $45,000, and for Hispanic families, it was about $61,000-$62,000. [1, 5, 10] Federal Reserve data confirms these large disparities, showing the typical white family had about six times the wealth of the typical Black family and five times that of the typical Hispanic family in 2022. [6] Although the absolute dollar-value gap in wealth between white families and Black and Hispanic families grew between 2019 and 2022, the wealth of the typical Black and Hispanic family saw a greater percentage increase during that period. [6] <9> The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) released its 'Society at a Glance 2024' report on June 20, 2024, which provides an overview of social indicators across member countries. [1] The report finds that among OECD countries, the United States has one of the highest levels of income and wealth inequality. [3] It specifically highlights that household wealth is significantly more concentrated than income, with the top 10% of households in the United States owning 79% of the country's total household wealth. [3] In comparison, the average for OECD countries is 52%. [3] Income inequality in the U.S. was also noted as among the highest in the OECD, alongside Chile, Costa Rica, and Türkiye. [3]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) is scheduled to release its annual report on Union Membership, covering data for the year 2024, on January 28, 2025, at 10:00 AM ET. This report provides key data on unionization rates across different industries and demographic groups in the United States. The previous report for the year 2023 was released on January 23, 2024. [2, 9] The data is a critical indicator for tracking labor's collective bargaining power and its influence on wage inequality. [8] <2> Oxfam released its annual report on global inequality, titled “Takers not Makers: The unjust poverty and unearned wealth of colonial inheritance,” to coincide with the World Economic Forum's meeting in Davos on January 20, 2025. The report reveals that in 2024, global billionaire wealth surged by $2 trillion, a rate three times faster than in 2023. It predicts that the world could see its first five trillionaires within the next decade. Oxfam argues that a significant portion of this wealth is unearned, with 60% stemming from inheritance, monopoly power, or cronyism. The report connects this modern inequality to historical colonial exploitation, noting that systems continue to extract wealth from the Global South. The analysis also highlights the situation in the United States, where it suggests a "billionaire president" could exacerbate inequality through tax cuts for the wealthy. <3> A Pew Research Center report published on January 9, 2025, reveals widespread global concern over economic inequality, with a median of 54% of adults across 36 nations viewing the gap between the rich and the poor as a "very big problem." The study, which surveyed 18 high-income and 18 middle-income countries, highlights significant ideological divisions on the issue within the United States. The U.S. fieldwork for the survey was conducted from April 1 to April 7, 2024. In the U.S., 76% of liberals consider economic inequality a very big problem, compared to just 30% of conservatives. This 46-percentage point difference represents the largest left-right ideological gap found among the countries surveyed. <4> The Institute for Policy Studies (IPS) released its 2024 year-end review on December 18, 2024, detailing significant victories against economic inequality. A key achievement highlighted was the defeat of Washington state's Initiative 2109 on November 5, 2024, which sought to repeal the state's capital gains tax on the wealthiest 0.2% of residents. [2, 3, 4, 5] This victory preserved a 7% tax on capital gains exceeding $250,000, which funds education and childcare programs. [3, 6] Additionally, the review celebrated successful ballot initiatives in multiple states. In the November 2024 election, voters in Alaska and Missouri approved measures to raise the minimum wage to $15 per hour, and alongside Nebraska, also passed initiatives to provide paid sick leave for workers. [7, 8, 9, 10] The summary also noted a new federal rule implemented by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), effective October 1, 2024, which allows state and local governments to give preference to contractors that create high-quality jobs when awarding federally funded projects. [12] An article by Sarah Anderson of IPS on November 15, 2024, also celebrated these state-level victories. [13] <5> The World Bank has updated its Poverty and Inequality Platform (PIP) as of September 2024, with the data forming the basis for the forthcoming 'Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2024'. A significant enhancement in this update is the inclusion of 'nowcast' estimates for poverty at the country, regional, and global levels through 2024 for the first time. The updated database now contains nearly 2,400 surveys with the addition of 16 new country-years. This release also introduces new methodologies for gauging global poverty and new indicators for shared prosperity, such as the 'Prosperity Gap'. The 'Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2024', which was released on October 15, 2024, provides the first comprehensive assessment of global progress on poverty and shared prosperity since the COVID-19 pandemic. The report indicates that while global poverty reduction has resumed, the pace is slower than before the pandemic. It highlights that nearly 700 million people are living in extreme poverty (less than $2.15 a day), and progress has stalled due to slower economic growth and other crises. <6> On October 10, 2024, the Social Security Administration officially announced a 2.5 percent cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2025. This increase will impact more than 72.5 million individuals receiving Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits. Starting in January 2025, the average Social Security retirement benefit is set to increase by approximately $50 per month. <7> An analysis of Bureau of Economic Analysis and Census data by the Progressive Policy Institute (PPI) suggests a potential decrease in income inequality in the United States. The PPI report highlights that the national Gini coefficient, a standard measure of income distribution, peaked at 0.494 in 2021 before falling to 0.489 in 2022 and 0.485 in 2023, the lowest figure recorded since 2017. [8] This aligns with U.S. Census Bureau data which also reported a decrease in the Gini index to 0.488 in 2022 from 0.494 in 2021, marking the first decline since 2007. [8] Furthermore, the PPI analysis shows that the income share of the bottom three quintiles of the population rose from 24.8% in 2021 to 25.5% in 2023. <8> Under Executive Order 14026, the minimum wage for federal contractors was scheduled to increase to $17.75 per hour, effective January 1, 2025. [4] <9> The U.S. Census Bureau released its 2023 data on income, poverty, and health insurance on September 10, 2024. The data showed that real median household income rose to $80,610 in 2023, a 4.0% increase from 2022 and the first significant annual rise since 2019. The official poverty rate decreased to 11.1% in 2023, down 0.4 percentage points from the previous year. However, the Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM), which considers government aid and necessary expenses, increased for the second consecutive year, rising to 12.9% from 12.4% in 2022. The percentage of the U.S. population without health insurance for all or part of 2023 was 8.0%, which was not a statistically significant change from the 7.9% rate in 2022. The press kit for the release included a variety of reports and analyses on these findings.

metadata.original_text: This time series records income inequality data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2025-12-21 to 2026-03-08. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> Visual Capitalist published an analysis mapping U.S. income inequality by state. The report highlighted that Washington, D.C., and New York exhibited the most severe income disparities nationwide, with Gini coefficients reaching 0.52. <2> On November 17, 2025, the Economic Policy Institute published a report outlining a new roadmap on tax policy. The report calls for stand-alone tax increases on the ultra-rich, specifically including a wealth tax on the top 0.1%, in order to combat corrosive economic inequality in the United States. <3> On November 15, 2025, approximately 200 protesters marched through San Francisco's affluent Pacific Heights neighborhood. The demonstration, part of a 'People Over Billionaires' day of action, was organized by members of labor and community groups to highlight extreme income inequality and denounce corporate tax breaks, as well as immigration crackdowns. <4> Oxfam America released new research highlighting a rapidly surging wealth gap in the United States. The report reveals severe economic disparities, demonstrating that since 1989, the richest 1% of U.S. households have grabbed at least 987 times more wealth per household than the bottom 20%. <5> The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis announced on July 31, 2025, that for the month of June 2025, personal income increased by $71.4 billion, which is a 0.3% monthly rate increase. [1] Concurrently, disposable personal income (DPI), the income remaining after taxes, rose by $61.0 billion (0.3%). [1] Personal consumption expenditures (PCE), a measure of consumer spending, also went up by $69.9 billion (0.3%). [1] The increase in personal income was primarily due to rises in government social benefits and compensation. [3] Personal savings were reported to be $1.01 trillion for the month. [3] <6> In its advance estimate, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported that real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 3.0 percent in the second quarter of 2025, which covers April, May, and June. This growth marked a rebound from the 0.5 percent decrease in the first quarter and surpassed expectations of a 2.4 percent rise. The expansion was primarily driven by a significant decrease in imports and an increase in consumer spending. <7> The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) announced in its advance estimate that the nation's real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 3.0 percent for the second quarter of 2025. This marks a significant rebound from the 0.5 percent decrease observed in the first quarter of 2025. The growth in the second quarter was primarily driven by a decrease in imports and an increase in consumer spending. These factors were partially offset by decreases in investment and exports. The release also noted that the price index for gross domestic purchases saw a smaller increase in the second quarter compared to the first. This advance estimate is the first of three that the BEA will release for the second quarter, with subsequent, more complete estimates scheduled for release in the following months. <8> Universal Basic Income (UBI) pilot programs are gaining momentum across the United States, with local governments and nonprofit organizations experimenting with this alternative to traditional welfare. As of early 2025, citizens in 18 states and the District of Columbia have participated in some form of a basic income study. According to the Stanford Basic Income Lab, which tracks these initiatives, there were 57 basic income experiments ongoing as of late January 2025. Later in the year, by August 2025, the Lab's count had increased to over 160 projects in the U.S. alone, though many of these are noted as being small in sample size. Proponents of UBI suggest it provides a financial floor and helps address economic inequality and the impacts of automation. However, critics and some study results point to more lackluster outcomes, with mixed results on employment, health, and well-being, suggesting that while the money is helpful, it may not be as transformative as advocates hope. <9> An analysis by the Budget Lab at Yale, based on tariff data through July 27, 2025, found that U.S. tariffs implemented in 2025 will increase consumer prices by 1.8% in the short term. This is equivalent to an average income loss of $2,400 per household. The report identifies the tariffs as a regressive tax, disproportionately impacting lower-income households, which face an estimated annual loss of $1,300. The analysis highlighted significant short-term price hikes for specific commodities, including a 39% increase for leather products and shoes and a 37% increase for apparel. Over the long term, these prices are expected to remain 18% and 17% higher, respectively. <10> On July 4, 2025, President Trump signed into law the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' (H.R. 1), a significant tax and spending package. [1, 2, 4] The legislation makes many provisions from the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act permanent, such as the pass-through entity deduction and 100% first-year bonus depreciation. [3] It also introduces new tax changes, including deductions for tips and overtime pay, an increased State and Local Tax (SALT) deduction cap of $40,000 through 2029, and indexing the Child Tax Credit for inflation. [4, 5, 21] According to the Bipartisan Policy Center, the bill is projected to cost $3.4 trillion over the next decade, and more than $4.1 trillion when accounting for interest on the national debt. [4] The bill is partly paid for through spending cuts and changes to programs such as Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), and student loans. [4] The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities states that these changes will disproportionately harm Black households by cutting benefits, while providing substantial tax giveaways to corporations and wealthy individuals. [12, 16] Analyses also point to over $1 trillion in spending cuts to healthcare, which could result in millions losing health insurance coverage. [13]
